In essence, it's a book on body language, and a pretty good one.

The elephant in the room: why would Scott Adams (cartoonist of Dilbert) recommend this book over more well-known authors on body language such as the work of Allan and Barbara Pease, who've more or less made a career out of the subject, or Paul Ekman, whose work was the foundation for the TV series Lie to Me? You'd have to ask Adams, but I can take a good guess: because all other things being equal, if you're going to consult an expert on the subject of a skill, consult the expert who uses and has to use his skill constantly in his day to day work.

Pease on his own bio is an "author and motivational speaker", with a career path of musician to life insurance salesman to "author and motivational speaker". He has no qualifications in psychology, neuroscience, or psychiatry. His material on body language, while scientific, is not derived from his own papers or experiments.

Navarro is (or was) a cop. Specifically, he was a FBI agent for 25 years - even more specifically, their top agent in the area of nonverbal communication. His specialty was behaviour and counterintelligence, and he was using these skills in real life investigations. That is, Navarro, unlike Pease, has actually had to put his money where his mouth is, and many incidents he describes in the book derive from his own working experience with the principles involved. He has, and cites, his own academic papers he's authored in the course of the book (along with many, many others. The field of body language is pretty well-supported by science, as the volume of papers on the subject suggests.)

Another point in favour of Navarro's book is that he's prepared to speak against his own interest. For all the hundreds of cases he's worked on over the years, all the research he's done, all the suspected criminals he's gone up against, he freely admits there is no magic bullet in body language to determine whether someone is lying or not. He's made mistakes in assessing body language and puts them out there in the book itself. Body language can reveal general states of emotion, or states of whether the person is comfortable or not, but the body does not say "I am lying." The body at best says things like "I'm stressed", or "I want to get out of here", or "I'm confident". What one infers from those observations is another thing entirely - though Navarro does suggest that not as much attention gets paid to comfort/discomfort signals in body language, in that depending on the question, these can be telling.

Navarro also doesn't suggest the insights he has on body language instantly turn you into a Bene Gesserit Truthsayer. The first thing he suggests is that to get the most benefit out of these observations, you have to learn to observe people consciously. This is not something we're trained to do, but without that application, Navarro's work is little more than a group of interesting insights.

If you're new to the concept of body language, the book with contain a lot of very big surprises. Even if you're passingly acquainted with it it will still contain a lot of stuff you haven't seen before. And because it's coming from a guy who actually used the material over many years, it'll be a bit more credible and practical than from more theoretical students of the discipline.

It's a non-fiction book, so voice is a lot less relevant, but it's amusing to sort of "feel" how Navarro writes. I'd use the phrase "unapologetic G-man, short back and sides haircut" to describe how he writes. That said, he also comes across as a decent man too -- so far as that's relevant.

The book is a handy element in the arsenal of anyone who needs to convince others, or work out what others are thinking. Less sprawling than Pease's work and more practical. Well worth a read.
